questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose to go to The Netherlands during my semester abroad because I wanted to go somewhere where the population spoke English at a high level of proficiency (without being native speakers). I chose to go to Amsterdam specifically because of its vibrant art scene and the many rich cultural influences from the consistent influx of people from all over the world. I chose the University of Amsterdam because they offer a lot of courses in English and are renowned for their academic standards.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The overall rating of my semester abroad is affected by the fact that the academic level at the University of Amsterdam was lower than I had expected, and by the fact that the housing provided by the University of Amsterdam through the company Lieven de Key was really poor.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The international office at University of Amsterdam was really good at sending out updates detailing what to expect upon arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received assistance from the international office at the University of Amsterdam in terms of filling out the forms in Mobility Online, and then there was a general introduction to the university approximately one week after my arrival. In the week before, there was the introductory week hosted by Erasmus Student Network (ESN Amsterdam), which consisted of a range of activities throughout the days and the evenings; some related to the university and others more related to living in Amsterdam.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It might have been nice to have the general introduction to the university a bit earlier on, and also perhaps to have been more properly introduced to the many different campuses around the city before having to make one's way to classes.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I lived off campus, but I received housing through the university. I applied and was “lucky" enough to be granted housing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The off campus housing in Zuiderzeeweg provided by the University of Amsterdam through the company Lieven de Key is quite far from the city center, the university campuses, and is generally quite isolated.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The off campus housing in Zuiderzeeweg provided by the University of Amsterdam through the company Lieven de Key was really quite poor. It was almost in total disrepair. It consisted of several blocks of shipping containers that had been transformed into single bedrooms with a small bathroom and a kitchenette. My room came equipped with a single bed, a large table, two rusty chairs, a damaged book case, and a worn-out closet space. The kitchen was equipped with a small refrigerator, a microwave, and a stovetop. Everything else you either had to bring yourself or buy. Upon arrival my room was extremely dirty and the walls had clearly not be painted for a while, seeing as they were completely covered with "lærer-tyggegummi". In addition to housing international students and exchange students, the tenancy at Zuiderzeeweg also hosts refugees, which means that as a resident you get the impression of having been designated to the periphery along with other people who have deemed undesirable by the people living in the city. A sentiment which is supported by the fact that the tenancy is located next to a large parking lot, a heavily trafficked road, and a building site.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: After being nominated by UCPH, I applied to the University of Amsterdam through their internal portal SiS. After I was accepted, I applied for courses through the same page.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: After being nominated by UCPH, I applied to the University of Amsterdam through their internal portal SiS. After I was accepted, I applied for courses through the same page.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I did not really require help during the registration process, but I am sure that I could have reached out to the international office at the University of Amsterdam had I had any questions or concerns.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had some trouble registering for courses at the University of Amsterdam. First of all, the course options available for MA level elective courses were quite limited. Second of all, many of the courses I was interested in had been placed in the same time slot, which meant that I ended up having to register for courses that I did not have an immediate interest in.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would urge future exchange students at the University of Amsterdam to be aware of the fact that the university schedules courses before the registration period begins, and that it is your responsibility as a student to ensure that the courses you have chosen do not overlap. You should also be aware of the fact that courses at UvA tend to have a smaller ECTS-load, which means that you have to register for more courses to meet the 30 ECTS per semester requirement than you do at UCPH during a single semester.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: As a master's degree student at UCPH, I would say that the MA elective courses offered at the University of Amsterdam correspond to first/second year bachelor's degree courses at universities in Denmark.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Because I was doing MA elective courses that were part of different study programs, I find it difficult to speak of a specific style of teaching. In some courses, we mostly had lectures, even though they were described as seminars. In other courses, we did a lot of assignments and presentations, which made it feel more like an independent study course than a “regular" university course. In the best one of the courses, I participated in, the teacher invoked the pedagogical principle of “old school is real school," which meant that we were discouraged from bringing our computers or other devices to class, but were instead asked to bring a notebook and a pen, to keep us from being distracted and make us more actively engaged in the subject matter. It seemed like an extraordinary measure, but it worked really well. Everyone participated much more freely, and the classes were much more interesting. It was also a bit of a challenge sometimes not being able to hide behind a screen, but having to look everyone in the eye. In the courses I participated in that revolved around museums / art / design, we went on a few excursions which added a practical dimension to the courses that is sometimes lacking at UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: During my semester abroad I was enrolled in the following courses: 1) Democracy and Distrust: An American Case History (6 ECTS), 2) Museums, Heritage and Digital Curation (12 ECTS), 3) Re-reading the Graphic Design Archive / Re-framing the Graphic Design Collection (6 ECTS), and 4) “Losing Earth"?: Activism and Diplomacy on the Environment and Climate since 1968 (6 ECTS).

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend that future exchange students at the University of Amsterdam enrol in the MA elective course “Losing Earth"?: Activism and Diplomacy on the Environment and Climate since 1968, which is taught by PhD Ruud van Dijk as part of the MA in History of International Relations. Ruud has taught the course independently or with a co-teacher from the MA in History of International Relations five times in total. It was really interesting to learn more about various (political) approaches to climate change during the twentieth century (and sometimes going back to the late nineteenth century). It was especially interesting to participate in the course because everyone had different academic backgrounds and different ways of understanding diplomacy/activism and the nature of climate change.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: When we would go on excursions during courses at the University of Amsterdam, students were expected to pay for transportation and entrance fees on their own. In general, the cost of public transportation in The Netherlands was a bit of a surprise.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Rent and transportation was definitely more expensive than I had anticipated, but groceries were less expensive than I had initially thought (compared to inflation-level prices in Denmark). Museum tickets are quite expensive even if one purchases a Museumkaart, which provides free or discounted museum tickets all over The Netherlands (only in state-funded museums!).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All kinds of cultural, athletic, and social activities were available for students at the University of Amsterdam. At CREA near the Roeterseiland Campus, it was possible to sign up for crafts courses, language courses, music courses, and all kinds of athletic activities for a monthly fee (similar to Danish "aftenskole"). Unfortunately, many of the courses had already started when I arrived in Amsterdam, and the next ones on offer would go beyond the duration of my semester abroad. Still, it was possible to participate in any number of activities, if one did not mind that the courses had already started.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definitely encourage future exchange students to visit some of the many museums in Amsterdam and in other Dutch cities. I would also recommend visiting some of the many parks in the city (especially during the summer!). I would recommend that you walk or ride a bicycle around the city, seeing as it really is the best way to get to know it. Riding a bicycle in Amsterdam does take a bit of courage - even if you are used to riding a bicycle in Copenhagen.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would similarly encourage future exchange students to visit some of the many museums in Amsterdam and in other Dutch cities during the weekends or holidays. Specifically, I would recommend a visit to designer Piet Hein Eek's studio in Eindhoven, which features a large collection of his furniture and also his factory. It is free of charge and most interesting if you have an interest in art / design. I would also recommend a visit to the beach Bloemendaal aan Zee whenever you need a break from the city (whether for a walk in the winter or a swim in the summer). Personally, I am a bit of a culinary enthusiast, so I would also recommend that you try some of the many wonderful cafés and restaurants for lunch or dinner.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: During the introductory week, the university staff spoke a lot about the experience of culture chock. I must admit that I did not immediately see the relevance of talking about culture chock, as I consider the Dutch culture and the Danish culture to be quite similar. However, I have to admit that I did struggle a bit during the second- and third month of my semester abroad. Because of the block system at the University of Amsterdam (the fact that you have several small courses of a short duration during the semester), I found it really difficult to connect with my fellow students, and I felt a little lonely from time to time. A bit out of sync with everyone else.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The Dutch are quite direct and very forward, which can come across as rudeness/impertinence.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated the cultural diversity of Amsterdam, even though I did find it a bit disheartening that cultural minorities tend to live in specific parts of the city.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) The academic level at the University of Amsterdam is not what you are used to at UCPH (to say nothing of the weird Dutch grading system), but do try to make the most of it anyhow. If nothing else, do enjoy that you have the time to cultivate academic- and non-academic interests on the side. Use your time wisely - in a way that is meaningful to YOU. 2) Choose courses whose subject matter go beyond your primary academic interests. 3) Do NOT accept housing from the University of Amsterdam in Zuiderzeeweg through the company Lieven de Key (!!), even if it means that you have to struggle to procure housing yourself.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The Dutch grading system is very different from the Danish. In The Netherlands you are given a grade between 1-10 (with up to one decimal point), and what constitutes a passing grade differs from one course to the other (usually 5.5 or higher depending on the teacher). Your final grade is usually made up of four components, including active participation/attendance, an interim essay, one or more presentations during the course, and a final essay at the end of the course. Also, your teacher is the only one to review your performance (there is no “censor" to ensure fair treatment, so you have to keep in your teacher's good graces).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was getting to know the city of Amsterdam. I find that it is always really rewarding and empowering in a sense to experience the sensation of being able to put a life together in a context different from the one you are used to.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge was having to settle for courses that were outright dissatisfactory, and housing that was also extremely disappointing.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
